extracted.intended_audience: students of rhetoric, orators, speechwriters and writers of forceful/classical prose
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing a forcible/oratorical style of composition using classical rhetorical figures and compositional choices (abrubtness, repetition, metaphor, etc.). Focus is on spoken or emphatic written discourse for persuasion and denunciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: aposiopesis (abrupt silence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The figure “aposiopesis” — a sudden breaking off in speech — contributes to force by leaving something unsaid and implying it dramatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use abrupt silence to suggest emotion or something too weighty to finish; it partakes of the same character as other abrupt figures and increases force. No specific anti-pattern given here beyond overuse implied.

rubrics_metrics.name: prosopopoeia / personification (speaking in another's voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The figure prosopopoeia (personification): speaking in the person of another (ancestors, homeland, a woman’s form) to reproach or dramatize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employing another voice can make a passage more vehement and dramatic (example: Plato’s Funeral Oration speaking as ancestors). Use to dramatize reproach and lend energy to style.

rubrics_metrics.name: figures of thought vs figures of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures of thought (e.g., prosopopoeia, aposiopesis) and figures of language should be used as described to produce force; both kinds help delivery and debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use figures of thought for energy in content, and figures of language for stylistic force; select appropriate figures per rhetorical aim. Distinguish ends: elevated vs forcible style use similar devices for different effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: ingenious choice of figures of language
rubrics_metrics.description: The more ingeniously the figures of language are chosen, the more forcible discourse can be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select figures (metaphor, anaphora, redoubling, etc.) with ingenuity; examples follow in text. Beware of clumsy or overused devices which weaken force.

rubrics_metrics.name: redoubling (repetition of a proper name)
rubrics_metrics.description: Redoubling — repeating a proper name (e.g., “Thebes, Thebes, our neighbour-state, has been torn from the heart of Greece”) — has a powerful effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition of a name for emphasis and emotional impact; can be a simple and striking forceful device.

rubrics_metrics.name: anaphora / epanaphora (repetition at clause beginnings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anaphora (repetition of the same word at the commencement of each clause) creates force, especially in combination with other figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine anaphora with asyndeton and homoeoteleuton for cumulative force (example: “against yourself you summon him; against the laws you summon him; against the democracy you summon him”).

rubrics_metrics.name: asyndeton (absence of conjunctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of conjunctions (asyndeton) sharpens cadence and increases force by making clauses strike in sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use asyndeton to speed rhythm and produce abruptness; when combined with anaphora and homoeoteleuton it yields a cumulative effect. Avoid inserting conjunctions which tame the force.

rubrics_metrics.name: homoeoteleuton (recurring termination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of a recurring termination or phrase-end (homoeoteleuton) contributes to the cumulative force of a passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeating phrase-endings in tandem with anaphora and asyndeton to create momentum and echo; beware mechanical or monotonous repetition without purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: clustering figures for cumulative force
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of figures (anaphora + asyndeton + homoeoteleuton) produces a cumulative force greater than each alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for interplay of devices rather than isolated use; rewriting to a smooth single clause (losing the figures) will usually diminish force.

rubrics_metrics.name: abruptness (both figure and compositional scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abruptness causes force: short, sudden elements and abrupt composition (including larger-scale disruption of rhythm) create energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use abrupt phrases, broken rhythm, or fragmented structure to convey anger or attack; large-scale abrupt composition (as Hipponax did by shattering verse) suits invective. Overdoing abruptness can produce a rough or unpleasant style.

rubrics_metrics.name: climax / gradatio (ascending series)
rubrics_metrics.description: The figure called 'climax' (gradatio) — a sentence that climbs higher and higher — intensifies force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange clauses in ascending importance (example from Demosthenes). Rewriting as a simple recital (flat summary) robs the passage of force. Use for building pressure toward a point.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid over-linking with conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: If words are tied together by conjunctions they become tamer; the absence of conjunctions preserves abruptness and force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer parataxis/asyndeton in forcible style; excessive smoothing through conjunctions reduces energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: metaphor for vigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor can be used to gain force in forcible style (e.g., ‘Python was blustering and rushing upon you in full flood’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose vivid metaphors that compress complex action into striking imagery; caution: ensure clarity so force does not become obscure.

rubrics_metrics.name: simile—use sparingly and briefly
rubrics_metrics.description: Similes can lend force (example: decree causing danger to pass by even as a cloud), but detailed comparisons do not suit the forcible style owing to their length and finish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer short, striking similes; avoid long, elaborate comparisons which produce beauty and finish rather than sharpness (antipattern: long gallant-hound boar simile).

rubrics_metrics.name: compound words to lend vigour
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound words (earth‑ward‑hurled, slant‑shelving) formed by usage lend vigour and immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use forceful compounds where appropriate to create concentrated imagery and momentum; avoid forced or opaque coinages.

rubrics_metrics.name: picturesque/idiomatic verbs and phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Picturesque expressions (e.g., 'elbowed his way through', 'hewed his way through', 'wormed his way') create vividness and force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose verbs and idioms that capture bodily action and motion for energetic expression; match the verb's tone to the subject (violence vs guile).

rubrics_metrics.name: discreet use of elaborate language
rubrics_metrics.description: A discreet use of elaborate language produces dignity as well as vigour; elaborate phrasing should be used with discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ elevated diction sparingly to add weight without lapsing into pomposity; aim for a balance between ornate and sharp expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: rise in tone for denunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: A deliberate rise in tone (a mid-exaltation increase) is used not to dignify but to make the style forcible when denouncing an opponent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tonal rise strategically at moments of denunciation; it amplifies force when placed amid exaltation.

rubrics_metrics.name: addressing questions to the audience (cross-examination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forcible effect may be achieved by asking questions of the audience without revealing the speaker's view, forcing the hearer into a corner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhetorical questions to pressure or expose inconsistencies; avoid converting the question into a mere statement of fact which loses the cross-examining force.

rubrics_metrics.name: epimone (dwelling/lingering on an idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: The figure 'epimone' (dwelling, lingering; elaboration beyond the bare statement) greatly contributes to force (example: 'Men of Athens, a terrible disease has fallen upon Hellas').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat or elaborate a core phrase to deepen emotional impact; beware of redundancy—epimone should intensify, not bore.

rubrics_metrics.name: euphemism as a source of force
rubrics_metrics.description: Euphemism (making inauspicious things appear auspicious) can produce a certain force or rhetorical advantage (example: 'seek the co-operation of the Victories' instead of 'cut up the Victories').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use euphemistic phrasing to soften an unpleasant proposal while still implying its harshness; can make a proposal more palatable and cunningly forceful. Overuse risks obscuring meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: innuendo, allegory, and hyperbole (Demadean vigour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Innuendo, allegorical expressions, and hyperbole can produce a thrilling and forcible effect (e.g., implying the whole world would have 'scented' a corpse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices create emotional shock and suggestiveness but carry dangers (coarseness, excess, burlesque). Use with poetic discretion and awareness of tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: covert allusion (veiled language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Covert allusion (veiled or indirect reproach) depends on good taste and circumspection; effective for censuring dangerous or powerful figures without explicit accusation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ covert hints when direct censure is risky (despots, powerful democracies). Ensure tact: the hint must be clear enough to the audience but circumspect to avoid reprisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: equivocal / ambiguous wording for ironic suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: Using words with an equivocal meaning can produce censures that seem unintentional or generate a puzzling ambiguous tone (example: Aeschines on Telauges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguity can suggest irony or double-meaning to provoke thought or mockery; however, it can leave listeners puzzled—use deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: indirect praise as admonition (praise to instruct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complimenting someone else for virtues the audience lacks (praising Gelo or Hiero) is a way to admonish without direct censure, prompting emulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use praise of exemplars to motivate audience behavior gently—especially useful before powerful persons or in delicate contexts. Avoid seeming sycophantic.

rubrics_metrics.name: choose rhetorical manner to fit aim (Aristippean, Xenophontic, Socratic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different manners (Aristippean asseveration, Xenophontic precept, Socratic interrogative) shape persuasion: asseveration, precept, or elenchic questioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the manner matching your rhetorical aim: Aristippean for firm asseveration, Xenophontic for didactic precept, Socratic for leading the interlocutor to self-awareness. Use Socratic questioning to corner an opponent subtly.

rubrics_metrics.name: smoothness vs clang (clashing vowels for force)
rubrics_metrics.description: Smoothness of composition (avoiding vowel concurrence) suits certain styles (Isocrates) but is not wholly suited to forcible language; clashing vowels can increase force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow deliberate clashing and roughness where anger or vigor is to be conveyed; excessive polish suggests elegant trifling rather than genuine passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: spontaneity / unpremeditated diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Words that seem spontaneous or unpremeditated often give an impression of vigour, especially in anger or outrage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive artificial smoothing that makes speech appear calculated; allow some spontaneity for authenticity and force.

rubrics_metrics.name: large-scale disruption of rhythm for invective
rubrics_metrics.description: Destroying regular rhythm (as Hipponax did) can make verse or prose suitable for energetic invective rather than eulogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use broken rhythm to match the satirical or invective purpose; do not use regular melodious rhythm when the aim is to attack harshly.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid unpleasant style pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'unpleasant' faulty style arises from repulsive subject-matter (disgusting details), disjointed composition (members unlinked), and long breathless periods which cause aversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dwelling on disgusting physical details in public discourse; ensure cohesion between members and vary sentence length to prevent breathless long periods that induce satiety or aversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid overly detailed comparisons in forcible style
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed comparisons and extended similes suit beauty and finish but are contrary to the aim of forcible style which should be sharp and short.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for forcible effects, refrain from long, elaborate comparative passages—keep comparisons terse and punchy.
